alternative: Serialize async work per key with a promise-chain mutex (Map<key, Promise>) or the async-mutex library; where the runtime exposes it use the Web Locks API (navigator.locks.request with a lock name derived from the key); SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics.wait/notify only when worker threads genuinely share memory.
idiom_name: per-key async mutex (promise queue) instead of striped OS locks
implementation_notes: The main thread runs one task at a time, so plain objects have no data races and a striped lock array has nothing to protect; the real hazard is interleaved async steps, which is handled by serializing per key: keep a Map of key to promise and chain each operation onto the previous one (or use async-mutex). Where coordination must cross tabs or workers, the Web Locks API provides named locks (navigator.locks.request) that fill the role of stripes without a lock array. Worker threads that share memory must use SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics.wait/Atomics.notify, because Atomics provides no mutex primitive. Stripe arrays are not idiomatic and are absent from the platform.
pitfalls: A keyed promise chain leaks the map entry unless it is deleted when the chain drains, and a rejection left unhandled can poison every later operation on that key.
Atomics.wait blocks the thread and is illegal on the main thread; only Atomics.waitAsync (or a worker) can wait there.
Web Locks are scoped to an origin and to secure contexts, and they coordinate tabs and workers of the same origin - using user-controlled strings as lock names couples unrelated code.
